units.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) conditions a language model on passages retrieved from an external collection at answer time.
Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) showed that separately trained question and passage encoders are effective for open-domain question answering.
Both systems take the passage as given.

In practice every document must first be divided into retrievable chunks, and that division fixes the granularity of everything downstream: whether a definition and the condition that limits it are retrieved together, whether an exception travels with its rule, and how much text the generator must read to find one fact.
Fixed-size chunking remains common because it is simple and makes index size predictable, but its boundaries need not coincide with changes of topic or argument.
Smaller chunks are more focused yet sever links between neighbouring statements; larger chunks keep those links but dilute the evidence.
Dense X Retrieval made this trade-off concrete by showing that both retrieval accuracy and downstream answer quality depend on the retrieval unit.
Longer context windows do not remove the problem, because models use evidence less reliably when it is buried among irrelevant text.

Prior work attacks the problem from several directions: lexical-cohesion segmentation, learned topic-boundary detectors, proposition-level retrieval units, contextualised chunk embeddings, and hierarchical or graph representations built over the corpus.
Most of these methods either train a boundary detector, change the retrieval unit, or add a representation layer.
Less explored is the direct use of the dynamics of local semantic change: how large a change is, whether it is accelerating, and how much it fluctuates within a short window.

We ask whether these quantities can serve as one control signal for two decisions that are usually designed separately, namely where to cut and what neighbouring context to attach, without assuming that a single granularity or a single context policy suits every region of every document.
STP-RAG treats the cosine displacement between adjacent unit embeddings as semantic velocity, its positive change as acceleration and its local spread as volatility.
Structural cues such as headings and paragraph breaks are added because they often mark real boundaries even when embeddings move only slightly.

We test whether one compact, interpretable profile can steer several representation decisions while every chunk remains traceable to its source offsets; fixed-size and learned segmenters remain the baselines it must beat.
A pilot implementation was run before this specification was written.
Our audit of that pilot, reported here, found that its comparisons are confounded by unequal prompt-token budgets, a structurally contaminated baseline, small generation samples and dropped queries.
We therefore present the pilot as descriptive evidence and use it to motivate a confirmatory design.
The research questions are framed for that design:
RQ1. Under a matched prompt-token budget, do acceleration, volatility, structure and selective context improve retrieval or answer quality over velocity-only and fixed-size baselines?
RQ2. How much of an observed quality difference is explained by chunk count, retrieved tokens and prompt tokens rather than by where the boundaries fall?
RQ3. Is the effect of selective context stable across multi-hop Wikipedia questions and long-document scientific questions, and which evidence properties predict it?
The paper makes four contributions:
A reference specification of STP-RAG with every parameter, interval convention and numerical safeguard stated, including an explicit mapping from the profile to the context policy (Section 3).
A component-level reconciliation of the specification with the audited pilot code, which identifies where the pilot differs and which components no reported number can validate (Section 4).
The pilot aggregates with corrected arm labels, absolute answer counts and a prompt-token account showing that the pilot cannot separate segmentation quality from evidence volume (Section 6).

A pre-specified confirmatory protocol with primary hypotheses, matched budgets, factorial ablations, competitive baselines, mechanism metrics and paired inference, implemented in an open evaluation harness (Section 5).
Section 2 reviews related work.
Section 3 defines the method, Section 4 audits the pilot, Section 5 gives the confirmatory protocol, Section 6 reports the pilot results, and Section 7 discusses limitations and concludes.
Retrieval and generation: RAG and DPR made dense evidence retrieval a standard ingredient of generation, but both treat the passage inventory as fixed.
Adaptive-RAG, Self-RAG and CRAG adapt retrieval behaviour at query time through routing, self-reflection and correction respectively, leaving the documents unchanged.
STP-RAG acts earlier, on how documents are cut and augmented before any query arrives, and is complementary to these methods.
Text segmentation: TextTiling places boundaries at valleys of lexical cohesion, C99 clusters a ranked sentence-similarity matrix, and TopicTiling scores boundaries from topic-model distributions.
Supervised and transformer segmenters learn boundaries from labelled context, and kernel change-point methods detect distribution shifts in a representation space.
P_k and WindowDiff evaluate a hypothesised segmentation against a reference independently of any downstream task.
Semantic velocity is closest to similarity-based segmentation; the STP adds second-order and dispersion terms, and none of these segmenters couples its boundaries to a context policy for retrieval.
Retrieval units and context: Dense X Retrieval compares propositions, sentences and passages and finds different retrieval–generation balances for each.
Late Chunking encodes a long text once and pools token embeddings into chunks so that each chunk embedding carries surrounding context.
RAPTOR builds a tree of recursive summaries and GraphRAG an entity graph with community summaries; both add generated structure above the corpus at extra build cost.
Lost in the Middle shows that where evidence sits in a prompt changes how well it is used, which is one reason prompt volume must be controlled when comparing chunkers.
Evaluating RAG: Knollmeyer et al. survey evaluation dimensions, question types and metrics for RAG and argue that retrieval and generation must be measured separately.
Mereu et al. compare five language models in a sparsely documented technical domain and find that the benefit of retrieval varies by model and saturates with retrieval depth.
Both support reporting retrieval depth, context volume and per-stage metrics rather than a single answer score, which our protocol adopts.
Table 1 summarises how STP-RAG differs from these lines of work.
We evaluate on HotpotQA, multi-hop questions whose supporting facts span several Wikipedia paragraphs, and QASPER, information-seeking questions answered from full scientific papers.
The two differ in document length, structure and evidence form, which makes them a useful contrast for RQ3.
This section is a reference specification.
It is deliberately complete so that an independent implementation produces the same chunks; Section 4 states which parts the pilot implemented.
Table 2 lists every parameter.
A document is an ordered sequence of sentence units D=(u_1,…,u_n), each stored with its section, paragraph and character offsets.
Progression is measured in units, p_i=i, so Δ p_i=1; another base unit or progression may be used only if it is declared and held constant across all compared methods.
Each unit is encoded by a frozen encoder and L_2-normalised, giving e_i∈R^d.
Semantic velocity is the cosine displacement between neighbours,
which lies in [0,2] and is dimensionless because Δ p_i=1.
Unit length enters later as a constraint, not as a divisor.
Positive acceleration records the onset of a steeper change,
with a_2^+=0.
Clamping at zero matters: immediately after a velocity peak the signed acceleration becomes strongly negative, and that drop should not be counted as evidence for a boundary.
The signed value is kept for diagnostics only.
Volatility is the population standard deviation of velocity over a trailing window of at most w valid values,
where v_W_i is the window mean.
The window is truncated, not padded, near the start of a document, and σ_2=0.
The population form is used because W_i is a fixed local neighbourhood, not a sample from which a global variance is estimated.

Placement: Two systems are possible and must be declared.
In branch A the augmented chunk c_i is embedded and indexed, so context changes retrieval.
In branch B base chunks are embedded and indexed, and context is attached only after retrieval, so it changes the prompt but not the ranking.
Figure 1 shows both.
Retrieval credit is always computed on base text; context tokens are counted in the prompt budget in both branches.
